question: A 5-year-old boy is brought to the emergency department by his mother because of a 2-hour history of word-finding difficulty, speech slurring, and weakness and sensory loss of his right arm and leg. He has not had fever, nausea, headache, or diarrhea. His mother reports an episode of severe pain and soft tissue swelling of the dorsum of his hands and feet when he was 12 months old, which self-resolved after 2 weeks. His temperature is 37.7°C (99.8°F), pulse is 90/min, and blood pressure is 110/80 mm Hg. Pulse oximetry on room air shows an oxygen saturation of 91%. He follows commands but has nonfluent aphasia. Examination shows marked weakness and decreased sensation of the right upper and lower extremities. Deep tendon reflexes are 2+ bilaterally. Babinski sign is present on the right. An MRI scan of the brain shows signs of an evolving cerebral infarction on the patient's left side. Which of the following is the most appropriate initial step in management?
reasoning_chain: CHAIN: "Word-finding difficulty, speech slurring, weakness, sensory loss in right arm and leg" -> "Symptoms suggestive of a stroke" -> "Nonfluent aphasia, right-sided weakness and sensory loss" -> "Localization to the left hemisphere of the brain" -> "MRI showing evolving cerebral infarction on the left side" -> "Acute ischemic stroke" -> "Need for urgent management" -> 90%
analysis: The presentation of a 5-year-old boy with word-finding difficulty, speech slurring, weakness, and sensory loss of right arm and leg, along with a history of previous soft tissue swelling episodes and an evolving cerebral infarction on MRI, is concerning for sickle cell disease with a high risk of stroke. The most appropriate initial step in management would be to start chronic transfusion therapy to prevent further strokes.
